paragraphs.text: Candlelight We forget how painfully dark the world once was. A candle – a good candle – provides barely a hundredth of the illumination of a single 100 watt light bulb, and yet candles provided most of the world's artificial illumination before the arrival of electricity.

Candles were of two types - tallow and wax. Tallow, made from animal fat, had the great advantage that, as it could be made at home as a by-product of any animal which also supplied food to eat, it was plentiful and cheap. But tallow candles melted extremely quickly and had to be frequently replaced, they burned with an uneven light, and also they smelled very unpleasant. Far superior in all these respects were candles made of beeswax. These gave a steadier light, but they cost about four times as much, and tended to be used only on special occasions.

Oil lamps Before the advent of electricity, for those who could afford it, oil lamps were the most efficient option, but the cost was prohibitive for most people, and oil lamps were dirty and needed cleaning daily. Even over the course of an evening, a lamp might lose 40% of its illuminating power as its glass chimney accumulated an increasingly thick layer of black soot.

Until the late 18th century, the quality of oil lighting had remained unchanged for some 3,000 years. But in 1783 a Swiss physicist named Ami Argand invented an oil lamp that increased lighting levels dramatically by ensuring more oxygen reached the flame. The Argand lamp also came with a knob, a novelty that allowed the user to adjust the flame's level of brightness. The best oil light was produced by whale oil, and the best type of whale oil was spermaceti from the head of the sperm whale. However, getting such oil was a difficult and dangerous business and by the 1850s, a gallon (4.55 litres) of whale oil sold for $2.50 – half the average weekly wage.

Gas lighting For the well-to-do in many large cities, gas was an additional option from about 1820. Mostly, however, it was used in businesses and for street lighting, and didn't become common in homes until closer to the middle of the century. Gas had many drawbacks. Those who worked in gas-supplied offices or visited gas-lit theatres, for example, often complained of headaches and nausea. To minimise that problem, gas lights were sometimes erected outside windows to light the interior. If installed indoors, they tended to blacken ceilings, discolour fabrics, corrode metal and leave greasy marks on every horizontal surface. Gas also needed some care in use. Most gas-supply companies reduced gas flow through their pipes during the day when demand was low. So anyone lighting a gas jet during the day had to open the tap wide to get a decent light. But later in the day as the companies increased the gas flow, the light could flare dangerously, scorching ceilings or even starting fires, wherever someone had forgotten to turn down the tap.

Gas had one irresistible advantage, however. It was bright – at least compared with anything else the pre-electric world knew. The average room with gas was 20 times brighter than without it. It provided wonderful overall illumination. At home in the evening, people read more and stayed up later. It is no coincidence that the mid-19th century saw a sudden and lasting boom in newspapers, magazines, books and sheet music.

Electricity One natural phenomenon known to science by the early 19th century had the promise to eliminate most of the dangers and shortcomings of candles and gas: electricity. Electricity had great potential, but it was hard to devise practical applications for it. Then, in 1846, rather unexpectedly, a man named Frederick Hale Holmes, patented an electric arc light. Holmes' light was made by generating an electric current and forcing it to jump between two carbon rods, the result being a blindingly bright light. Arc lighting, however, was never a huge success because it was expensive and needed constant attention to run smoothly. In the early 1870s, Hermann Sprengel, a German chemist working in London, came up with a device that proved crucial to making electrical household illumination possible. Sprengel found that he could decrease the air in a glass chamber to one-millionth its normal volume. This meant that light inside the chamber could shine for hundreds of hours. All that was needed was to find a suitable material for the 'filament' which would glow inside it.

The most determined search was undertaken in 1877 by Thomas Edison, already America's most renowned inventor. After trying out a large number of possibilities from the far corners of the world, Edison finally hit upon a piece of thread which had been carbonised. This treatment seemed to work successfully and the light would burn for many hours. When Edison's first practical installation came it was lastingly significant. He wired a whole district of New York City and, on the afternoon of 4 September 1882, Edison operated a switch that illuminated 800 electric bulbs in 85 businesses that had signed up to his scheme. By modern standards those first lights were pretty feeble, but to people of the time the electric light appeared miraculous.
